text: Everything you built over the last three lessons -- pillar scores, documented gaps, before-and-after outcome metrics -- is necessary, and still not sufficient, for an executive audience. A board member doesn't care, in the moment, what phishing-resistant MFA is or why Advanced beats Initial. They care whether the organization's exposure to a costly incident is going down, and whether the money spent on the program is producing that result.

So every finding gets run through the same three questions before it reaches that audience. What risk went down, in plain terms -- not 'we deployed PAM,' but what that actually prevents. What would the business impact have been without it -- a concrete counterfactual, not an abstraction. And is the trend moving the right direction, and how fast -- because a single snapshot just invites the question 'is that good,' while a trend line answers it without anyone having to ask.

Here's that pattern on a real finding. Technically: standing domain admin accounts dropped from 200 to 3. Translated: if an attacker steals one employee's credentials today, the number of systems they could immediately control dropped by over 98 percent, and most access now has to be requested and expires in 30 minutes. Same fact, no acronym, and a sentence anyone can repeat back accurately.

Same pattern again. Technically: mean time to detect simulated lateral movement dropped from 4 days to 22 minutes. Translated: if an intruder gets a foothold, we now expect to catch them before they reach a second system in almost every case -- previously, they had days to operate before anyone noticed. That's the test for every translation: would a non-technical reader repeat it back correctly five minutes later?

For a recurring update, resist showing the full pillar scorecard live -- save that for an appendix. Use one slide with four fixed elements: a headline risk-reduction statement built from your strongest metric, a trend line across the last several reporting periods instead of one snapshot, what's funded next and specifically why, tied to the gap actually driving remaining risk, and one honest sentence naming the biggest exposure that's still open.

That last element matters more than it looks like it should. A program that only ever reports good news loses credibility the moment something finally goes wrong. Naming the real gap yourself, before an auditor or an incident does it for you, is what keeps this kind of reporting trusted -- and what keeps the budget funded long enough to close it. That closes out Chapter 6; Chapter 7 turns this same discipline toward sequencing the roadmap itself.
